summary:
Laura is a 49-year-old female presenting with a BMI of 24.3, following a ketogenic, very low-carbohydrate diet rated 7 out of 10 for quality with a volume of 6 out of 10. She does one cardio session a week, no resistance training, and walks 5,000 to 7,500 steps a day. She sleeps less than six hours most nights. She reports brain fog, low mood or anxiety, weight gain or difficulty losing weight, and low energy that she says is not normal for her. Her goals are to build muscle, improve her mood and improve her energy.

Her sugar handling, read from the markers that reflect weeks and months rather than a single moment, is excellent: HbA1c 33 against a limit of 42, fructosamine 257, urine glucose negative, and a triglyceride to HDL ratio of 0.49 that is about as insulin-sensitive as it gets. Her fasting glucose on this sample is reported as 1.60, and the insulin and C-peptide as low; those three do not fit the rest of the picture and should be repeated on a fasted morning sample before anything is read into them. Her cortisol of 56 is a late-afternoon value against a range written for the morning, which is why it reads low.

The finding that explains how she feels is a folate deficiency, and it is one of the most satisfying things a blood test can find because it is so fixable. Her serum folate is 2.7 against a limit of 3.0 and an ideal of 8 or more. Her red cell folate, which reflects the last three to four months and cannot be blamed on a single meal, is 489 against a limit of 523, confirming a true deficiency. Her red cells have already responded: the mean cell volume is 105.2 against a limit of 100, which is called macrocytosis, meaning the cells are being built too large, and the haemoglobin concentration inside them is 301 against a limit of 320. Her haemoglobin of 128 is still fine, so she is not anaemic, but that is the next step if nothing changes. Homocysteine at 11.4 is above the ideal of 9 for the same reason. Folate comes almost entirely from leafy greens, pulses, beans and fortified grains, and a strict ketogenic diet removes most of those; the body’s store lasts a few months, which fits a diet she has presumably held for a while. Brain fog, low mood and tiredness that feels out of character are the textbook symptoms, and there is a specific reason for that: folate is needed to make the neurotransmitters behind mood and focus, and to build red cells that carry oxygen efficiently, so a shortage shows up in the head before it shows up in the blood count. The fix does not require abandoning the diet. Two large handfuls of spinach, rocket or kale a day, plus asparagus, broccoli, avocado and Brussels sprouts at dinner, cover the daily requirement inside a ketogenic carbohydrate budget, and a prescription course of folic acid restores the stores far faster than food alone can. Her B12 is 384 with an active B12 of 70.7, adequate rather than abundant, and because folate should never be replaced without B12 alongside it, both go in the plan. Expect the fog and mood to lift within three to six weeks of starting, and the red cell size to normalise over about three months as the oversized cells are replaced. Thyroid, alcohol (GGT 9.2) and pernicious anaemia (intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies negative) are excluded as causes. Coeliac disease is negative, with the caveat that the test is only reliable in someone eating gluten.

The finding that needs a prompt response is the D-dimer. It is 972 against a limit of 500. D-dimer is a breakdown product of blood clots, and it rises when the body is forming and dissolving clot somewhere. It does not diagnose a clot on its own, and it rises for other reasons too: recent injury or surgery, infection, pregnancy and high oestrogen. Her hsCRP is undetectable, so infection is not the reason. Her oestradiol is 647, a healthy mid-cycle level, but oestrogen does raise clotting tendency. The right response is not alarm but not dismissal either: a repeat D-dimer through her GP within days, and if it remains raised, an ultrasound of the legs. That is a quick, painless scan, and it is the standard way this question gets answered; most people who reach it are told there is nothing there. If the repeat comes back under 500, the question is closed and nothing further is needed. If she has any leg swelling or pain, chest pain, breathlessness or coughing blood in the meantime, that is same-day care. It is also worth her knowing that oestrogen-containing contraception or HRT, long flights, immobility and dehydration all push in the same direction, so if any of those apply they belong in the GP conversation.

Now the part of this report that deserves as much attention as the two findings above, because it is most of the panel: a great deal is going very well, and some of it is impressive for 49.

Her heart and arteries are in excellent shape. Total cholesterol is 4.50, LDL 2.56, HDL 1.59, triglycerides 0.78, and ApoB, the protein that counts the artery-damaging particles and the single best predictor of cardiovascular risk, is 73 mg/dl, comfortably within the ideal. Small dense LDL, the most harmful sub-type, is 25.4 and ideal. Her total to HDL ratio of 2.83 and ApoB to ApoA-I ratio of 0.42 are both deep in the low-risk zone. This is a genuinely good lipid profile, and it is worth saying that on a ketogenic diet it is not a given: LDL often climbs on high-fat eating, and hers has not. Her Cardiovascular Risk Score, a TrueVitals index from 0 to 100 built from ApoB, LDL, HDL, triglycerides, Lp(a), hsCRP and HbA1c with no age term, is 35, in the acceptable band, and the only input holding it above the ideal of 20 is Lp(a) at 40.2. Lp(a) is an inherited cholesterol particle that lifestyle does not change; hers is within the laboratory range and only mildly above ideal, a small inherited tendency worth knowing once, and the answer to it is exactly what she is already doing, keeping ApoB low. Every cardiac muscle marker is as clean as it can be: troponin T undetectable, CK-MB undetectable, myoglobin 5.19, FABP-3 1.55. There is no heart muscle stress of any kind.

Her inflammation is, in effect, zero. hsCRP is below 0.30, the lowest the assay reads, and MCP-1, the chemical signal that draws inflammatory cells into fat tissue and artery walls, sits at the very bottom of its range. For a woman of 49 this is an excellent result, and it is the strongest evidence on the panel that her diet is not doing any quiet damage.

Her kidneys are excellent: cystatin C 0.82, creatinine 51.3, an eGFR of 111, uric acid 156, and no albumin detectable in her urine, which is the earliest possible sign of kidney strain and is absent. Her liver is excellent on every enzyme: ALT 20.0, AST 20.3, GGT 9.2, ALP 52, bilirubin 8.0, albumin 45.7, and the fibrosis indices are as low as they go. A GGT of 9.2 also quietly rules out alcohol as a cause of her large red cells. Her thyroid is working well, with a TSH of 1.16 in the sweet spot, FT4 17.2, and both thyroid antibodies negative, with anti-TPO at 9.82 below the limit but not zero, worth a recheck in a couple of years. Her iron stores are healthy with a ferritin of 81, so iron is not part of the fatigue. Vitamin D at 108 is excellent, B2 is adequate, and her antioxidant capacity is where it should be. Her immune system is balanced, with IgG, IgA and IgM all normal, complement normal, and every autoimmune antibody negative: no lupus, no rheumatoid arthritis, no coeliac disease, no autoimmune gastritis. All nine cancer screening markers, including CA 125, CA 15-3 and CEA, are within range. Her HbA1c of 33 says her blood sugar over the last three months has been excellent, and a triglyceride to HDL ratio of 0.49 says her insulin sensitivity is about as good as it gets.

Her hormones show a woman whose ovaries are still fully active at 49: FSH of 2.96 and LH of 1.6 are low, oestradiol of 647 and a low progesterone of 2.94 describe a mid-cycle, pre-ovulatory sample, and there is no sign of the menopause transition on this draw. SHBG is 97.8, within range but above the 90 ideal; high mid-cycle oestrogen and a very low-carbohydrate diet with low insulin both raise it, and a high SHBG lowers the free testosterone available to muscle, which matters for her goal of building it. Prolactin at 367 is within range but above the 300 ideal, and less than six hours’ sleep most nights is the likeliest reason. Testosterone and DHEA-S are ideal.

Her stated goal of building muscle deserves its own reading of the results, because the panel says quite a lot about it. Testosterone at 0.673 is within the ideal range for a woman, but SHBG at 97.8 binds most of it, leaving a free androgen index of 0.69 at the low end: the raw material is there, but less of it is reaching muscle than the total suggests. Urea at 2.77 is below the ideal floor, which usually means protein intake is modest, and creatine kinase at 33 sits at the bottom of its range, which is what no resistance training looks like on a blood test. IGF-1 at 19.1 is ideal, so the growth signal is healthy. Put together: she has the hormonal foundation to build muscle, but she is not currently giving it the two things it needs, which are enough protein (around 105 grams a day at her weight) and a training stimulus. Two short resistance sessions a week would change the CK, the SHBG and the urea within a couple of months, and they are also the most reliable lever she has on mood and sleep.

Short sleep runs through this report more than any single marker. Less than six hours most nights is an independent cause of brain fog and low mood that no supplement corrects, and it leaves traces here: prolactin above ideal, neutrophils and white cells above ideal with no inflammation to explain them, and a cortisol rhythm that a single afternoon sample cannot judge. Folate replacement will do a great deal for how she feels, but if the sleep stays at six hours the improvement will plateau below where it should. The lifestyle section treats sleep as the second priority for that reason.

Her results at 49 also deserve a word about what they say for the next few years. FSH at 2.96 and oestradiol at 647 describe ovaries that are still fully cycling, with no biochemical sign yet of perimenopause on this sample. That is one snapshot, and FSH in particular swings across a cycle, so it does not rule the transition out; it does mean that the mood, sleep and energy symptoms she reports are better explained by folate and sleep than by hormones right now. If cycles become irregular or symptoms change character over the next year or two, a repeat of FSH, LH and oestradiol on days two to five of a cycle would be the right test. Her vitamin D of 108, calcium of 2.25 and PTH of 2.1 are a strong bone foundation for that stage, and resistance training protects it further.

The remaining findings are minor and mostly diet-shaped. Ketones are present in her urine and free fatty acids (NEFA) are 0.93, marginally above the limit: both are the expected and intended state of a ketogenic diet, not a concern with a normal HbA1c and bicarbonate. Bicarbonate at 21.6 and potassium at 3.96 sit a fraction under their ideals for the same reason. Zinc at 11.2 is within range but just above the limit and below the 12 ideal, copper at 13.9 is at the low end, magnesium at 0.87 is at the low end of ideal, and urea at 2.77 is below ideal, which usually reflects a modest protein intake. Together they read as a diet that is doing its job on sugar and fats and quietly running short of the micronutrients that come from plants. TIBC at 44.6 is fractionally under its limit with a ferritin of 81, which is not an iron finding. Neutrophils at 5.73 are above ideal with no inflammation, consistent with short sleep. IL-8 and HB-EGF are reported above range and IL-15 below, with no inflammatory signal anywhere else on the panel to support them; they are variable markers and carry no weight against an undetectable hsCRP. Vitamin D at 108 is excellent. Every cancer screening marker is within range. The Epstein-Barr antibodies show a past infection only.

Connecting the symptoms to the results: brain fog, low mood and out-of-character tiredness with a folate of 2.7, a red cell folate below range and red cells already enlarged is a clean match, and folate replacement typically lifts these within a few weeks. Short sleep is an independent contributor that no supplement fixes, and it also explains the prolactin. The difficulty losing weight is less well explained by the bloods: her metabolism is healthy on every stable marker, so the levers are sleep, resistance training and the protein intake that the low urea hints is modest. The one thing this panel leaves open is her fasting glucose and insulin, which should be repeated on a fasted morning sample.

Two findings drive this report, and they are unrelated to each other. The first is a folate deficiency that explains her symptoms. Serum folate 2.7 and red cell folate 489 are both below range, and the red cells have responded with a mean cell volume of 105.2 and a haemoglobin concentration of 301; homocysteine at 11.4 is raised for the same reason. Thyroid, alcohol and autoimmune causes are all excluded, which leaves the diet: a strict ketogenic pattern removes most folate-rich foods, and a few months is all it takes for stores to run down. B12 at 384 with active B12 at 70.7 is adequate rather than abundant and must be replaced alongside the folate. Brain fog, low mood and tiredness that feels wrong are exactly what folate deficiency produces, and they are exactly what she reported.

The second is a D-dimer of 972 against a limit of 500, which stands apart from everything else. Nothing else on the panel points to a clot: platelets are normal, hsCRP is undetectable, cardiac markers are all clear. A mid-cycle oestradiol of 647 is a plausible contributor, but a D-dimer at this level cannot be closed by reasoning. It needs a repeat through her GP within days, and symptoms in the meantime mean same-day care.

The fasting glucose of 1.60, with insulin 10.2 and C-peptide 0.79, does not fit her HbA1c of 33, negative urine glucose, triglycerides of 0.78 and ApoB of 73, all of which say her metabolism is healthy. Those three need a fasted morning repeat before anything is concluded from them, and nothing about them should worry her in the meantime. The cortisol of 56 is a late-afternoon value against a morning range.

What has been excluded is worth stating. Her cardiovascular picture is strong, her kidneys and liver are excellent, her thyroid is normal, her iron stores are healthy at a ferritin of 81, every cancer screening marker is within range, and coeliac disease, H. pylori, lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and pernicious anaemia are all negative. Her ovaries are still fully active with no sign yet of the menopause transition. The loose ends are the mild inherited Lp(a) of 40.2, worth knowing once, the anti-TPO of 9.82 that is negative but not zero, and the cluster of low-normal micronutrients (zinc, copper, magnesium, potassium) and low urea that describe a diet strong on fats and sugar control and short on plants and protein.

The four-month retest will tell the whole story in a handful of numbers. Folate and red cell folate back in range and MCV under 100 confirm the deficiency is corrected and explain any improvement in fog and mood. Homocysteine below 9 follows. A D-dimer under 500, if it has not already been repeated, closes the clotting question. Urea above 3 and creatine kinase rising into the middle of its range are the signs that protein and training have started to do their work, and SHBG drifting down towards 90 means more of her testosterone is reaching muscle. A fasted 9am glucose and insulin close the one gap this sample left. Everything else on this panel is a baseline worth keeping rather than a problem worth fixing.
lifestyle:
The honest picture: the ketogenic diet is doing what she asked of it, her sugar control and cholesterol are genuinely good, but it has quietly starved her of folate and is running zinc, magnesium, potassium and copper low. Those gaps, plus less than six hours’ sleep, are her brain fog, mood and energy. None of the habits below need her to abandon the diet; they put back what it removed.
Add two large handfuls of leafy greens to the first meal of the day, every day: spinach, rocket, kale or chard, wilted into eggs or eaten as a base. Anchor: greens go in the pan before the eggs. Why: greens are the richest keto-compatible source of folate, and folate is the deficiency behind her symptoms.
Add a serving of low-carbohydrate folate and mineral foods to dinner: asparagus, broccoli, avocado, Brussels sprouts, or a small portion of lentils or edamame if her carbohydrate budget allows. Anchor: half the dinner plate is green before the protein goes on. Why: this is where folate, potassium, magnesium and copper come from, and all four are low.
Put a palm-and-a-half of protein on the plate at every meal. Anchor: protein is the first thing chosen when planning any meal. Why: her urea of 2.77 says protein intake is modest, and building muscle at 49 needs about 1.6 grams per kilogram, roughly 105 grams a day for her.
Two twenty-minute resistance sessions a week, bodyweight or dumbbells, the same two days every week. Anchor: booked in the diary like an appointment. Why: it is the only thing that builds the muscle she wants, it lowers SHBG so more testosterone reaches muscle, and it improves sleep quality.
Fix a bedtime that gives seven and a half hours, and hold the wake time seven days a week. Anchor: phone on charge in the kitchen thirty minutes before the bedtime. Why: short sleep most nights is an independent cause of brain fog and low mood, it raises her prolactin, and no supplement corrects it.
Get outside within an hour of waking, even for ten minutes. Anchor: coffee goes in a travel cup and the first drink of the day is outdoors. Why: morning light sets the sleep drive for that night, which is the cheapest fix for a short sleeper.
Add a mineral-rich electrolyte to water once a day: a pinch of salt, and potassium and magnesium from food or a low-sugar electrolyte powder. Anchor: the first glass of water after waking. Why: ketogenic eating loses sodium, potassium and magnesium, and hers sit at the low end.
flags:
Fasting glucose 1.60 (range 4 to 7), insulin 10.2 (range 17.8 to 173), C-peptide 0.79 (range 1.1 to 4.4), HOMA-IR 0.10: inconsistent with HbA1c 33, fructosamine 257, urine glucose negative and TG/HDL 0.49. Repeat fasting glucose, insulin and C-peptide on a fasted 9am sample before interpretation. Cortisol 56 (range 69 to 345, morning range) on a late-afternoon draw; 9am repeat if clinically indicated. IL-8 257.7 (limit 240), HB-EGF 183.6 (limit 136), IL-15 0.73 (range 0.89 to 2.02) with hsCRP below 0.30: no supporting inflammatory signal.
D-dimer 972 (limit 500). No supporting signs of clot on the panel (platelets 278, hsCRP below 0.30, cardiac markers clear); mid-cycle oestradiol 647 is a plausible contributor. Repeat D-dimer via GP within days; if persistently raised, lower-limb ultrasound. Leg swelling or pain, chest pain, breathlessness or haemoptysis: same-day care.
Folate 2.7 (range 3 to 26.8) and red cell folate 489 (range 523 to 1257): folate deficiency, dietary (ketogenic). MCV 105.2 (limit 100), MCHC 301 (limit 320): macrocytosis without anaemia (Hb 128). Homocysteine 11.4 (ideal below 9). B12 384 (ideal 500 or above), active B12 70.7 at ideal floor. Thyroid normal, GGT 9.2, intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies negative. Replace folate with B12. Coeliac negative, valid only if consuming gluten.
Zinc 11.2 (ideal 12 to 18), copper 13.9 (ideal 14 or above), magnesium 0.87 (low end of ideal), potassium 3.96 (ideal 4.0 or above), urea 2.77 (ideal 3.0 or above). Micronutrient and protein shortfalls consistent with a restrictive ketogenic pattern.
Ketones (urine) 15 mg/dl, NEFA 0.93 (limit 0.9), bicarbonate 21.6 (ideal 22 or above): expected physiology of a ketogenic diet; no concern with HbA1c 33.
Lipoprotein (a) 40.2 nmol/L (ideal below 32). Mild inherited tendency; ApoB 73 mg/dl and LDL 2.56 ideal. Note once, no action.
SHBG 97.8 (ideal below 90) with FAI 0.69 at the low end; prolactin 367 (ideal below 300). Mid-cycle oestrogen, low insulin and short sleep. Morning repeat of prolactin when rested if symptoms persist.
Neutrophils 5.73 and WBC 8.79 above ideal with hsCRP undetectable; short sleep. NSE 19.98 within range. TIBC 44.6 fractionally low with ferritin 81, not an iron finding. Anti-TPO 9.82 negative but not zero; recheck in two years.
Epstein-Barr EBNA IgG and VCA IgG positive, VCA IgM negative: past infection, not active.
Reassuring negatives: HbA1c 33 and urine glucose negative; LDL 2.56, HDL 1.59, triglycerides 0.78, ApoB 73, small dense LDL 25.4 all ideal; troponin, CK-MB, FABP-3 and myoglobin clear; cystatin C 0.82, eGFR 111, urine albumin not detected; every liver enzyme ideal; TSH 1.16 with FT4 17.2; ferritin 81; vitamin D 108; all nine cancer screening markers within range; coeliac, H. pylori, ANA, RF, anti-CCP negative; ovarian function intact (FSH 2.96, oestradiol 647).
Not returned by the laboratory: leptin, resistin, IL-6, TNF-alpha, pepsinogens I and II, gastrin-17, cystatin C (urine), NGAL (urine), KIM-1, the FABP 4 to 9 series, the cytokine autoantibody series and a further set of interleukins and adhesion molecules. PhenoAge calculated with an assumed RDW of 13 percent because Randox does not report it.
recommendations:
D-dimer 972: book a GP appointment this week for a repeat D-dimer, and mention that the sample was taken mid-cycle with an oestradiol of 647. If it remains above 500, a lower-limb ultrasound is the usual next step. Any leg swelling or pain, chest pain, breathlessness or coughing blood before then: same-day care.
Folate deficiency with macrocytosis (folate 2.7, red cell folate 489, MCV 105.2): the GP will usually prescribe folic acid 5 mg daily for four months, with B12 checked or given alongside. Ask whether she was eating gluten when tested, because the negative coeliac result is only valid if she was; if not, the GP may want to repeat it or test differently.
Repeat fasting glucose, insulin and C-peptide on a fasted 9am sample, with a 9am cortisol at the same time. Nothing else on this panel suggests a problem with any of them; the repeat is to confirm it.
Prolactin 367 above ideal with short sleep: no action now; a rested morning repeat if low mood or cycle changes persist after sleep improves.
Lp(a) 40.2 above ideal: no treatment needed; keep ApoB and blood pressure well controlled long term and mention it if cardiovascular risk is ever assessed.
Anti-TPO 9.82, negative but not zero, with a perfect TSH: recheck thyroid function and antibodies in two years, sooner if fatigue persists after folate is corrected.
Targets: about 1,700 calories a day with 105 grams of protein and 25 grams of fibre from low-carbohydrate vegetables, built up over a few weeks. Retest in four months: folate, red cell folate, MCV, homocysteine, D-dimer (if not already repeated), B12, zinc and the fasting glucose set.
supplementation:
Folic acid: prescription-strength 5 mg daily for four months is the standard correction for a deficiency with macrocytosis, and that is a GP decision. If she prefers an over-the-counter route while waiting, methylfolate 1,000 mcg daily is the form to choose. Never take folate without checking B12, because folate alone can mask a B12 deficiency.
Vitamin B12 as sublingual methylcobalamin 1,000 mcg daily for three months, alongside the folate. B12 384 with active B12 at the ideal floor is adequate rather than abundant, and the two vitamins work together in the same pathway.
Zinc picolinate 15 mg daily with food for three months. Zinc 11.2 is just above the limit and below ideal; it supports mood, sleep and immunity, and restrictive diets run it low.
Magnesium glycinate 300 mg in the evening. Magnesium 0.87 sits at the low end of ideal, a ketogenic diet loses it, and the glycinate form supports sleep.
Electrolytes: a low-sugar potassium and magnesium electrolyte once a day, or the same from avocado, leafy greens, nuts and seeds. Potassium 3.96 and bicarbonate 21.6 are both a fraction under ideal for diet reasons.
Vitamin D: no supplement needed. At 108 she is well within the ideal range; if she takes one, keep the dose modest.
Omega-3 fish oil 1 to 2 grams of combined EPA and DHA daily is reasonable for mood on a diet that may be low in oily fish, but it should wait until the D-dimer question is settled, because omega-3 at higher doses mildly affects clotting.
Do not take iron; ferritin is 81 and iron stores are healthy. Do not take a multivitamin with high copper until zinc is corrected; the copper to zinc balance is fine as it is.
The most important changes are not supplements. They are two handfuls of greens at breakfast, half a plate of green vegetables at dinner, protein first at every meal, two resistance sessions a week, and seven and a half hours’ sleep.

biomarkers.name: TrueScore
biomarkers.description: Your TrueScore is 59 out of 100. Every marker is scored on how far it sits from its ideal range, combined by body system with the systems that matter most for long-term health weighted highest, and then capped by the most serious finding, so a result that needs a GP cannot be hidden by good numbers elsewhere. Fair. Raw 68.1; held to 59 by a system rated "See your GP". Weakest systems: immunology 26%, inflammation 33%, glucose & insulin 44%. Biggest drags: Glucose, Glucose (estimated from HbA1c, for calculation only), C-peptide, Cortisol.
biomarkers.low_causes: One or more systems well outside ideal, or a finding that needs a GP

biomarkers.name: PhenoAge
biomarkers.description: PhenoAge is a biological age estimated from nine blood markers (Levine 2018). Randox does not report red cell distribution width, so a typical value of 13 percent was assumed for that input, and the glucose input was taken from the HbA1c-estimated average because the fasting value needs repeating. It sits close to her calendar age of 49, held up slightly by the MCV of 105, and it will improve as the folate corrects.
biomarkers.high_causes: Inflammation, raised glucose, anaemia, kidney or liver strain, smoking

biomarkers.name: Cardiovascular Risk Score
biomarkers.description: The Cardiovascular Risk Score is a TrueVitals index from 0 to 100 built from ApoB, LDL, HDL, triglycerides, Lp(a), hsCRP and HbA1c, with no age term; 20 or below is ideal. At 35 it sits in the acceptable band (20 or below is ideal, 40 or below acceptable) with every input ideal except Lp(a) at 40.2, the one inherited factor to keep in mind. It is not a reason to act, only to keep doing what she is doing.
biomarkers.high_causes: Raised ApoB or LDL, high Lp(a), inflammation, raised HbA1c, smoking

biomarkers.name: Copper
biomarkers.description: Copper is a trace mineral for iron use and connective tissue. At 13.9 it is within the laboratory range but at the low end and just below ideal. A restrictive diet can run copper low; nuts, seeds, shellfish and dark chocolate cover it.

biomarkers.name: Total Antioxidant Status (TAS)
biomarkers.description: TAS measures the blood’s overall capacity to neutralise oxidative stress. At 1.50 it is within range and at the ideal floor.

biomarkers.name: Glutathione Reductase
biomarkers.description: Glutathione reductase recycles the body’s main antioxidant and reads riboflavin (B2) status. At 48 it is above the 33 limit, so B2 is adequate.

biomarkers.name: Zinc
biomarkers.description: Zinc supports immunity, mood and healing. At 11.2 it is within the laboratory range but just above the 10.7 limit and below the 12 ideal. Zinc is easy to run short of on a restricted diet, and low zinc contributes to low mood and poor sleep. Worth correcting.

biomarkers.name: Folic acid
biomarkers.description: Folate is a B vitamin needed for building red cells, DNA and the chemistry behind mood and energy. At 2.7 it is below the 3.0 limit and a long way below the ideal of 8. This is the finding of the report. Folate comes almost entirely from leafy greens, pulses, beans and fortified grains, which a strict ketogenic diet removes, and the body’s store lasts only a few months. Her red cells are already oversized because of it, her homocysteine is raised because of it, and brain fog, low mood and unusual tiredness are the classic symptoms. It corrects within weeks.

biomarkers.name: Vitamin B12
biomarkers.description: B12 works alongside folate. At 384 it is within the laboratory range but below the 500 ideal, and the active B12 confirms it is adequate rather than abundant. Because folate and B12 must be replaced together (folate alone can mask a B12 problem), both go in the plan.

biomarkers.name: Vitamin D
biomarkers.description: Vitamin D supports immunity, bone, mood and insulin sensitivity. At 108 it is well within the ideal range, an excellent result.

biomarkers.name: Active B12
biomarkers.description: Active B12 is the fraction cells can use. At 70.7 it sits exactly at the ideal floor: adequate, not abundant.

biomarkers.name: Red Cell Folate
biomarkers.description: Red cell folate reflects folate stores over the past three to four months, so it cannot be blamed on a single meal. At 489 it is below the 523 limit, confirming that the low serum folate is a true deficiency and not a bad day.

biomarkers.name: B12 Status
biomarkers.description: B12 384 and active B12 70.7, at the ideal floor. Intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies negative. To be replaced alongside folate.

biomarkers.name: Folate Status
biomarkers.description: Serum folate 2.7 (limit 3) and red cell folate 489 (limit 523), with MCV 105.2 and homocysteine 11.4. Dietary, from a ketogenic pattern. The finding of the report.

biomarkers.name: Vitamin D Status
biomarkers.description: Vitamin D 108, well within the 75 to 120 ideal. No supplement needed, and if she takes one the dose should stay modest.

biomarkers.name: Zinc Status
biomarkers.description: Zinc 11.2, just above the limit and below the 12 ideal; copper 13.9 at the low end too. Restrictive diet.

biomarkers.name: B2 (Riboflavin) Status
biomarkers.description: Glutathione reductase 48 against a limit of 33, the marker used to read riboflavin status. Eggs, dairy and meat cover B2 well on a ketogenic diet.

biomarkers.name: Oxidative Stress Assessment
biomarkers.description: Total antioxidant status 1.50 at the ideal floor and glutathione reductase 48. Adequate, helped by more plant intake.

biomarkers.name: Nutritional Assessment
biomarkers.description: Folate deficient with macrocytosis; B12, zinc, copper, magnesium and potassium at or below the low end of ideal; urea low suggesting modest protein. Vitamin D, B2 and iron good. A ketogenic diet that needs its plant side rebuilt.

biomarkers.name: Haemoglobin
biomarkers.description: Haemoglobin carries oxygen. At 128 it is within the ideal range, so despite the folate finding below she is not anaemic. Folate deficiency shows in the size of the red cells before it shows in the haemoglobin, which is exactly what this panel has caught.

biomarkers.name: Haematocrit
biomarkers.description: The share of blood volume made up of red cells. At 42.5 percent it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Mean Cell Haemoglobin (MCH)
biomarkers.description: The average haemoglobin per red cell. At 31.7 it is within the laboratory range but above the ideal, because her red cells are larger than they should be.

biomarkers.name: Mean Cell Haemoglobin Concentration (MCHC)
biomarkers.description: How densely the haemoglobin is packed inside each red cell. At 301 it is below the 320 limit. Large, less-concentrated red cells are the picture of folate or B12 deficiency, and her folate is low. The MCV below confirms the pattern.

biomarkers.name: Red Blood Cell Mean Cell Volume (MCV)
biomarkers.description: MCV is the average size of a red cell, and it is the finding that explains how she feels. At 105.2 it is above the 100 limit, which is called macrocytosis: her red cells are being built too large. The commonest causes are folate deficiency, B12 deficiency, alcohol and an underactive thyroid. Her thyroid is normal, her B12 is adequate, and her folate is below range with red cell folate low too. That is the cause, and it is one of the most fixable findings a blood test can produce.

biomarkers.name: Red Blood Cell Count
biomarkers.description: The number of red cells. At 4.04 it is within the ideal range, at the lower end: fewer, larger cells, which is what folate deficiency produces.

biomarkers.name: Basophil Count
biomarkers.description: Basophils are involved in allergic responses. At 0.10 they sit at the top of the laboratory range; a delayed sample can nudge white cell counts, and there is nothing else on the panel to suggest allergy.

biomarkers.name: Eosinophil Count
biomarkers.description: Eosinophils rise with allergy and parasites. At 0.06 they are ideal.

biomarkers.name: Lymphocyte Count
biomarkers.description: Lymphocytes hold immune memory. At 2.30 they are ideal. A healthy lymphocyte count also means the immune memory that fights viruses is well stocked.

biomarkers.name: Monocyte Count
biomarkers.description: Monocytes clear debris after infection. At 0.60 they are within range at the top of the ideal.

biomarkers.name: Neutrophil Count
biomarkers.description: Neutrophils are the first-response white cells. At 5.73 they are within the laboratory range but above the 4.5 ideal. With hsCRP undetectable there is no infection here; short sleep and a late-afternoon draw both raise neutrophils.

biomarkers.name: White Blood Cell Count
biomarkers.description: The total white cell count. At 8.79 it is within range but above ideal, in step with the neutrophils.

biomarkers.name: Platelet Count
biomarkers.description: Platelets form clots. At 278 they are ideal, which matters alongside the D-dimer result: there is no shortage of platelets being used up.

biomarkers.name: High Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hsCRP)
biomarkers.description: hsCRP measures low-grade inflammation. Below 0.30 it is as low as the assay reads: there is no inflammation in this picture at all, which is an excellent result and a useful anchor for reading the cytokines that the delayed sample disturbed.

biomarkers.name: Antistreptolysin O (ASO)
biomarkers.description: ASO detects antibodies from a recent streptococcal infection. At 50.1 it is negative.

biomarkers.name: D-Dimer
biomarkers.description: D-dimer is a breakdown product of blood clots, and it rises when the body is forming and dissolving clot somewhere. At 972 it is nearly double the 500 limit. This is the one result on the panel that needs a prompt response. A raised D-dimer does not diagnose a clot, and it rises for other reasons too (recent injury, surgery, infection, pregnancy, and a sample that has sat for a long time can push it up), but it cannot be dismissed without a repeat. If she has any leg swelling or pain, chest pain, breathlessness or coughing blood, she should seek same-day care. Otherwise, a repeat D-dimer through her GP within days, and if it remains raised, a scan.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin-5 (IL-5)
biomarkers.description: IL-5 drives eosinophils in allergic responses. At 0.35 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin-8 (IL-8)
biomarkers.description: IL-8 recruits neutrophils to sites of inflammation. At 257.7 it is reported above the 240 limit. With hsCRP undetectable, MCP-1 at the floor and no other inflammatory signal, there is no inflammation to explain it; IL-8 is one of the more variable cytokines and a repeat would be expected to settle.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin-15 (IL-15)
biomarkers.description: IL-15 supports natural killer and memory T cells. At 0.73 it is reported below the 0.89 limit. A slightly low IL-15 in isolation, with a normal lymphocyte count and normal immunoglobulins, has no clinical significance.

biomarkers.name: Epidermal Growth Factor (EGF)
biomarkers.description: EGF drives tissue repair. At 130 it is within range. It is reported for completeness; an EGF in range says the skin and gut lining are repairing normally.

biomarkers.name: Heparin-binding EGF-like growth factor (HB-EGF)
biomarkers.description: HB-EGF is involved in tissue repair and blood vessel remodelling. At 183.6 it is reported above the 136 limit. It is a variable marker without a specific clinical meaning at this level, and with an undetectable hsCRP it does not change the picture.

biomarkers.name: Monocyte Chemotactic Protein-1 (MCP-1)
biomarkers.description: MCP-1 draws monocytes into fat tissue and artery walls. At 130 it sits at the very bottom of the range, consistent with the absence of inflammation.

biomarkers.name: Granulocyte Macrophage Colony Stimulating Factor (GM-CSF)
biomarkers.description: GM-CSF stimulates white cell production. At 0.55 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin 17A
biomarkers.description: IL-17A drives psoriasis-type and some joint inflammation. Undetectable.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin 17F
biomarkers.description: IL-17F works alongside IL-17A. At 0.08 it is low. Together with the undetectable IL-17A it rules out the psoriasis-type inflammatory pathway.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin 22
biomarkers.description: IL-22 protects the gut and skin barrier. At 0.86 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: NLR
biomarkers.description: The neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio is a simple measure of inflammatory load. At 2.49 it is within range but above the 2.0 ideal, because neutrophils are high in range; with hsCRP undetectable this reflects short sleep and an afternoon draw rather than inflammation.

biomarkers.name: Inflammation Assessment
biomarkers.description: hsCRP undetectable and MCP-1 at the floor: no inflammation. D-dimer 972 is the exception and needs a prompt repeat. IL-8 and HB-EGF above range and IL-15 below are variable markers with no supporting signal.
biomarkers.result: None, one clotting marker to repeat

biomarkers.name: Interleukin-6 (IL-6)
biomarkers.description: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is part of the Signature panel but was reported by Randox as not available on this sample. hsCRP was returned and is undetectable.

biomarkers.name: Platelet:Lymphocyte Ratio
biomarkers.description: The platelet to lymphocyte ratio. Within range. Reported for completeness alongside the NLR.

biomarkers.name: Systemic Immune-Inflammation Index
biomarkers.description: The systemic immune-inflammation index. Within range, slightly above ideal from the neutrophils.

biomarkers.name: Monocyte:HDL Ratio
biomarkers.description: The monocyte to HDL ratio. Ideal. A low ratio pairs a normal monocyte count with a protective HDL.

biomarkers.name: Glucose
biomarkers.description: Fasting glucose is the sugar in the blood before eating. At 1.60 it is reported below the 4.0 limit. A value this low does not fit the rest of her results: her HbA1c of 33 says her average blood sugar over three months is excellent, her urine glucose is negative, and a person with a true glucose of 1.6 would be acutely unwell. It should be repeated on a fasted morning sample before any conclusion is drawn from it.

biomarkers.name: HbA1c
biomarkers.description: HbA1c is average blood sugar over the past three months, and unlike the fasting glucose it is not affected by how long the sample sat. At 33 it is well inside the ideal, an excellent result that says her sugar handling is healthy.

biomarkers.name: Insulin
biomarkers.description: Fasting insulin is the hormone that moves sugar out of the blood. At 10.2 pmol/L it is reported below the 17.8 limit. A very low-carbohydrate diet lowers insulin, and a low value alongside a healthy HbA1c and ideal triglycerides is not a concern in itself; because the glucose on this sample needs repeating, the insulin should be repeated with it.

biomarkers.name: Non-Esterified Fatty Acids
biomarkers.description: NEFA are free fatty acids released from fat stores. At 0.93 they are marginally above the 0.9 limit. On a ketogenic diet this is expected: the body is running on fat, and NEFA rise as fat is mobilised. It is the same signal as the ketones in her urine, and it is not a concern in this context.

biomarkers.name: C-peptide
biomarkers.description: C-peptide is released with insulin and shows how hard the pancreas is working. At 0.79 it is reported below the 1.1 limit. On a ketogenic diet the pancreas produces little insulin because little is needed, so a low C-peptide is the expected pattern; it should be repeated alongside the glucose and insulin.

biomarkers.name: Fructosamine
biomarkers.description: Fructosamine reflects average blood sugar over the past two to three weeks. At 257 it is within the laboratory range and just above the ideal, consistent with the HbA1c.

biomarkers.name: Adiponectin
biomarkers.description: Adiponectin is a hormone made by fat tissue that keeps the body insulin-sensitive. At 6.12 it is within range and just below ideal; it rises with weight loss and exercise.

biomarkers.name: Metabolic Assessment
biomarkers.description: HbA1c 33, fructosamine 257, urine glucose negative, TG/HDL 0.49: healthy glucose handling. Fasting glucose, insulin and C-peptide are reported low and do not fit the rest; repeat on a fasted morning sample.

biomarkers.name: HOMA-B
biomarkers.description: HOMA-B estimates pancreatic insulin output from fasting glucose and insulin. Both inputs need repeating on this occasion, so it is not calculated; it will be when the fasting set is repeated.

biomarkers.name: Glucose:Insulin Ratio
biomarkers.description: The glucose to insulin ratio depends on two markers that need repeating. To be calculated on the repeat.

biomarkers.name: TyG Index
biomarkers.description: The TyG index combines triglycerides and fasting glucose as a marker of insulin resistance. The fasting glucose needs repeating; her triglycerides of 0.78 and TG/HDL ratio of 0.49 already say her insulin sensitivity is good.

biomarkers.name: Adiponectin:Insulin Ratio
biomarkers.description: The adiponectin to insulin ratio depends on an insulin value that needs repeating. Adiponectin itself, at 6.12, is within range.

biomarkers.name: Estimated Average Glucose
biomarkers.description: Average glucose estimated from HbA1c, about 5.6 mmol/L. Healthy, and a better guide than a single fasting value.

biomarkers.name: Total Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: Total cholesterol is the sum of all cholesterol particles. At 4.50 it is at the ideal ceiling.

biomarkers.name: LDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: LDL is the cholesterol in the particles that deposit in artery walls. At 2.56 it is within the ideal, just under the 2.6 ceiling. On a ketogenic diet LDL often rises; hers has not.

biomarkers.name: HDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: HDL is the protective cholesterol. At 1.59 it is within range and effectively at the ideal.

biomarkers.name: Total Cholesterol / HDL Cholesterol Ratio
biomarkers.description: The ratio of total to protective cholesterol. At 2.83 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Triglycerides
biomarkers.description: Triglycerides are the fat particles in the blood between meals. At 0.78 they are ideal, which is typical of a very low-carbohydrate diet done well.

biomarkers.name: Apolipoprotein A-I
biomarkers.description: ApoA-I is the main protein on HDL particles. At 173 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Apolipoprotein B
biomarkers.description: ApoB counts the artery-damaging particles, and it is the best single measure of cholesterol risk. At 73 mg/dl it is within the ideal.

biomarkers.name: Apolipoprotein B / A-I Ratio
biomarkers.description: The ratio of damaging to protective particles. At 0.42 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Apolipoprotein E
biomarkers.description: ApoE is a transport protein involved in clearing fat particles. At 3.06 it is within range. This is the protein level, not the genetic type.

biomarkers.name: Small LDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: Small dense LDL are the LDL particles most likely to lodge in artery walls. At 25.4 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Lipoprotein (a)
biomarkers.description: Lp(a) is an inherited cholesterol particle that raises heart risk independently of diet and does not change with lifestyle. At 40.2 nmol/L it is within the laboratory range but above the ideal of 32. This is a mild inherited tendency rather than a high one, worth knowing once: it argues for keeping ApoB and blood pressure well controlled over the long term, which she is already doing.

biomarkers.name: Homocysteine
biomarkers.description: Homocysteine is an amino acid that rises when folate, B12 or B6 are short and damages blood vessels when high. At 11.4 it is within the laboratory range but above the ideal ceiling of 9, and her folate is deficient. This is the same finding seen from a different angle, and it should fall as the folate is replaced.

biomarkers.name: TG/HDL Ratio
biomarkers.description: The triglyceride to HDL ratio is a reliable stand-in for insulin sensitivity. At 0.49 it is ideal, and it is the best evidence on this panel that her insulin sensitivity is good, since the direct insulin markers were sample-affected.

biomarkers.name: Remnant Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: Remnant cholesterol is the cholesterol carried in triglyceride-rich particles. At 0.35 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Lp(a)-Corrected LDL
biomarkers.description: LDL with the Lp(a) contribution removed, about 2.3. Her modifiable LDL is already low.
biomarkers.high_causes: Diet high in saturated fat, familial hypercholesterolaemia

biomarkers.name: Atherogenic Index of Plasma
biomarkers.description: The atherogenic index of plasma from triglycerides and HDL. Ideal.
biomarkers.high_causes: High triglycerides, low HDL, insulin resistance

biomarkers.name: LDL:HDL Ratio (Castelli II)
biomarkers.description: Castelli risk index II, LDL divided by HDL. Ideal. Both inputs are within their ideal ranges.

biomarkers.name: Non-HDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: Non-HDL cholesterol, everything except the protective HDL. At 2.91 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: HDL % of Total
biomarkers.description: HDL as a share of total cholesterol. At 35 percent it is ideal.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low HDL or high total cholesterol

biomarkers.name: Castelli Risk Index I
biomarkers.description: Castelli index I, total to HDL cholesterol. At 2.83 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Atherogenic Coefficient
biomarkers.description: The atherogenic coefficient. At 1.83 it is ideal. Driven by a low non-HDL and a healthy HDL.

biomarkers.name: VLDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: VLDL estimated from triglycerides. At 0.35 it is ideal. Low triglycerides mean little VLDL leaving the liver, the intended effect of a low-carbohydrate diet.

biomarkers.name: LDL:HDL Ratio
biomarkers.description: LDL divided by HDL. At 1.61 it is ideal. Both inputs sit within ideal.

biomarkers.name: LDL Particle Count (estimated)
biomarkers.description: LDL particle number estimated from ApoB, about 730 nmol/L. Ideal.

biomarkers.name: Small LDL % of Total LDL
biomarkers.description: The share of LDL in small dense particles. Ideal. Her LDL is mostly the larger, less harmful kind.

biomarkers.name: Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1)
biomarkers.description: IGF-1 reflects growth hormone activity. At 19.1 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Cortisol
biomarkers.description: Cortisol is the main stress hormone and follows a strong daily rhythm: highest in the early morning, lowest in the evening. At 56 it is reported below the 69 limit. The laboratory range describes a morning sample, and this sample was collected in the late afternoon when cortisol is naturally low, so the value is consistent with a normal rhythm rather than a deficiency. If cortisol is ever in question, a 9am sample is the one to take.

biomarkers.name: Follicle Stimulating Hormone
biomarkers.description: FSH rises as the ovaries wind down. At 2.96 it is low, which at 49 means her ovaries are still fully active on this sample: no sign of the menopause transition yet. FSH varies across the cycle, so this is one snapshot.

biomarkers.name: Luteinising Hormone
biomarkers.description: LH triggers ovulation. At 1.6 it is within range and low, consistent with an early or mid-cycle sample.

biomarkers.name: Prolactin
biomarkers.description: Prolactin is a pituitary hormone that rises with stress and poor sleep. At 367 it is within the laboratory range but above the 300 ideal. Short sleep most nights is the likeliest reason, and a morning repeat when rested would settle it.

biomarkers.name: Dehydroepiandrosterone Sulphate (DHEAs)
biomarkers.description: DHEA-S is the adrenal building block for sex hormones. At 4.6 it is ideal for 49.

biomarkers.name: Testosterone
biomarkers.description: Testosterone in women drives libido, muscle and mood. At 0.673 it is within the ideal range.

biomarkers.name: Oestradiol
biomarkers.description: Oestradiol is the main oestrogen. At 647 it is within range and reflects a mid-cycle, pre-ovulatory sample: her ovaries are still producing well at 49. Oestrogen at this level raises SHBG and, together with the raised D-dimer, is relevant to the GP conversation about clotting.

biomarkers.name: Progesterone
biomarkers.description: Progesterone is the hormone of the second half of the cycle. At 2.94 it is low, consistent with a sample taken before ovulation.

biomarkers.name: Sex Hormone Binding Globulin
biomarkers.description: SHBG carries sex hormones. At 97.8 it is within the laboratory range but above the 90 ideal. High oestrogen at mid-cycle and a very low-carbohydrate diet with low insulin both raise SHBG, and it lowers the free fraction of testosterone available to muscle, which matters for her goal of building muscle.

biomarkers.name: Free Androgen Index
biomarkers.description: The free androgen index estimates active testosterone. At 0.69 it is within range and at the low end, because the SHBG is high.

biomarkers.name: Hormonal Assessment
biomarkers.description: FSH 2.96, LH 1.6, oestradiol 647, progesterone 2.94: mid-cycle, pre-ovulatory, no menopause transition on this draw. SHBG 97.8 and prolactin 367 above ideal. Cortisol 56 is a late-afternoon value against a morning range.

biomarkers.name: Testosterone:Cortisol Ratio
biomarkers.description: This recovery and stress index depends on a morning cortisol. Hers was a late-afternoon sample, so the ratio is not calculated.

biomarkers.name: Prolactin Recovery Post-PEG
biomarkers.description: Prolactin Recovery Post-PEG is part of the Signature panel but was reported by Randox as not available on this sample. Prolactin was returned within range, so the follow-on test is not needed.

biomarkers.name: Iron
biomarkers.description: Serum iron is the iron in transit and swings with meals. At 10.5 it is within the laboratory range but below ideal; a single afternoon value carries little weight, and ferritin is the marker that counts.

biomarkers.name: Ferritin
biomarkers.description: Ferritin is stored iron. At 81 it is well within the ideal range, so her iron stores are healthy and iron is not part of the fatigue picture.

biomarkers.name: Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC)
biomarkers.description: TIBC is the blood’s capacity to carry iron. At 44.6 it is fractionally below the 44.8 limit. With ferritin at 81 this is not an iron finding; TIBC falls slightly when protein intake is low or a sample has sat, and it needs no action.

biomarkers.name: Transferrin
biomarkers.description: Transferrin is the iron-carrying protein. At 2.00 it sits at the bottom of the range, in step with the TIBC, and for the same reasons.

biomarkers.name: Transferrin Saturation
biomarkers.description: The share of transferrin loaded with iron. At 23.5 percent it is within range and just below ideal.

biomarkers.name: Iron Status Assessment
biomarkers.description: Ferritin 81 ideal, haemoglobin 128, transferrin saturation 23.5 percent. TIBC 44.6 fractionally low is not an iron finding. No iron needed.

biomarkers.name: UIBC
biomarkers.description: Unsaturated iron binding capacity. Within range; iron stores are healthy.

biomarkers.name: Iron:TIBC Ratio
biomarkers.description: Iron divided by total binding capacity. Within range, just below ideal on a single afternoon iron value.

biomarkers.name: Total Protein
biomarkers.description: Total protein is albumin plus globulin. At 69.0 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Calcium (adjusted)
biomarkers.description: Calcium adjusted for albumin. At 2.25 it is at the ideal floor.

biomarkers.name: Chloride
biomarkers.description: Chloride tracks sodium and acid balance. At 102.9 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Magnesium
biomarkers.description: Magnesium is needed for energy, muscle and sleep. At 0.87 it is within the ideal, at the lower end. A ketogenic diet loses magnesium, and with short sleep and low energy it is worth keeping topped up.

biomarkers.name: Phosphate
biomarkers.description: Phosphate works with calcium in bone and energy metabolism. At 1.03 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Potassium
biomarkers.description: Potassium governs nerve and muscle electrical activity. At 3.96 it is within range and just below the 4.0 ideal; ketogenic eating lowers potassium, and leafy greens, avocado and nuts cover it.

biomarkers.name: Sodium
biomarkers.description: Sodium is the main blood electrolyte. At 138.4 it is ideal. Ideal sodium alongside a normal chloride says she was well hydrated at the draw.

biomarkers.name: Bicarbonate
biomarkers.description: Bicarbonate is the blood’s buffer against acid. At 21.6 it is within the laboratory range but just below the 22 ideal. A ketogenic diet produces mild ketone acids, and the ketones in her urine explain this; it is expected and not a concern at this level.

biomarkers.name: Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)
biomarkers.description: PTH regulates calcium. At 2.1 it is ideal. With calcium at the ideal floor and vitamin D at 108, calcium regulation is exactly where it should be.

biomarkers.name: Dickkopf-1 (DKK-1)
biomarkers.description: DKK-1 is a regulator of bone formation. At 1715 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Anion Gap
biomarkers.description: The anion gap checks for unmeasured acids. At 17.9 it is within range but above the 16 ideal: the ketone acids of a ketogenic diet account for it, and with a normal bicarbonate and HbA1c it is expected physiology.

biomarkers.name: Bone Assessment
biomarkers.description: Adjusted calcium 2.25, phosphate 1.03, PTH 2.1, DKK-1 1715, vitamin D 108.

biomarkers.name: Estimated Osmolality
biomarkers.description: Estimated osmolality uses the fasting glucose as an input, which needs repeating. Her sodium of 138.4 and urea of 2.77 are both normal, so hydration and concentration are not in question.

biomarkers.name: Albumin-Corrected Anion Gap
biomarkers.description: Anion gap corrected for albumin. Slightly above ideal from the ketone acids of a ketogenic diet; expected.
biomarkers.high_causes: Dietary acid load, reduced kidney clearance, ketosis, dehydration

biomarkers.name: Calcium:Phosphate Ratio
biomarkers.description: The calcium to phosphate ratio. Within the ideal range. Both minerals sit within their ideal ranges.

biomarkers.name: Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT)
biomarkers.description: ALT is the enzyme most specific to liver cells. At 20.0 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)
biomarkers.description: ALP comes from liver, bone and gut. At 52 it is ideal. A normal ALP with a normal GGT rules out any bile duct or bone turnover issue.

biomarkers.name: Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST)
biomarkers.description: AST is a liver and muscle enzyme. At 20.3 it is ideal. With ALT also ideal there is no liver or muscle strain to read.

biomarkers.name: Gamma-Glutamyltransferase (GGT)
biomarkers.description: GGT is the liver enzyme most sensitive to metabolic strain and alcohol. At 9.2 it is ideal and at the low end, which also makes alcohol an unlikely cause of her large red cells.

biomarkers.name: Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)
biomarkers.description: LDH is released during cell turnover. At 293 it is ideal. A normal LDH also argues against any red cell destruction, which matters given her enlarged red cells.

biomarkers.name: Glutamate Dehydrogenase (GLDH)
biomarkers.description: GLDH rises with liver cell injury. At 2.0 it is ideal. This is the most specific marker of liver cell damage on the panel, and it is as low as it gets.

biomarkers.name: Total Bilirubin
biomarkers.description: Bilirubin is the pigment from red cell breakdown. At 8.0 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Direct Bilirubin
biomarkers.description: The processed form of bilirubin. At 2.59 it is ideal. A normal direct bilirubin means bile is flowing freely from the liver.

biomarkers.name: Bile Acids
biomarkers.description: Bile acids reflect bile flow. At 2.90 they are ideal. Ideal bile acids rule out the cholestatic pattern that sometimes appears on high-fat diets.

biomarkers.name: Albumin
biomarkers.description: Albumin is the main protein the liver makes. At 45.7 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Globulin
biomarkers.description: Globulins are the antibody and transport proteins. At 23.3 they sit at the bottom of the range; with normal immunoglobulins this is of no concern.

biomarkers.name: Aldolase
biomarkers.description: Aldolase is a muscle enzyme. At 4.00 it is within range. A muscle enzyme in the low part of its range is consistent with no resistance training, which her goals may change.

biomarkers.name: Pancreatic Amylase
biomarkers.description: The digestive enzyme for starch. At 28 it is ideal. With lipase also ideal the pancreas is not a factor in anything on this report.

biomarkers.name: Lipase
biomarkers.description: The pancreatic enzyme for fat. At 39.0 it is ideal. A high-fat diet asks a lot of the pancreas, and hers is coping without strain.

biomarkers.name: A/G Ratio
biomarkers.description: The albumin to globulin ratio. At 1.96 it is within range and at the top of ideal, because globulins sit at the bottom of their range.

biomarkers.name: Liver Assessment
biomarkers.description: ALT 20.0, AST 20.3, GGT 9.2, ALP 52, bilirubin 8.0, albumin 45.7. Nothing to improve.

biomarkers.name: FIB-4 Index
biomarkers.description: FIB-4 estimates liver scarring. Very low; no scarring. Platelets, ALT and AST are all healthy, so the index is as low as it can be.

biomarkers.name: APRI
biomarkers.description: APRI, a second liver scarring index. Very low. AST and platelets are both ideal.

biomarkers.name: NAFLD Fibrosis Score
biomarkers.description: The NAFLD fibrosis score. Low-risk band. With a BMI of 24.3 and ideal liver enzymes there is nothing for this score to detect.
biomarkers.high_causes: Advanced fibrosis in fatty liver disease

biomarkers.name: AST:ALT Ratio (De Ritis)
biomarkers.description: The De Ritis ratio (AST to ALT). Close to 1 with both enzymes ideal; nothing to read.
biomarkers.high_causes: Alcohol-related liver disease, cirrhosis, muscle injury

biomarkers.name: R Factor
biomarkers.description: The R factor compares ALT and ALP patterns. Low; both enzymes ideal.

biomarkers.name: Microalbumin / Creatinine Ratio
biomarkers.description: The urine albumin to creatinine ratio detects the earliest leak of protein through the kidney filters. Not detected, which is the best possible result.

biomarkers.name: Creatinine
biomarkers.description: Creatinine is a muscle waste product cleared by the kidneys. At 51.3 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Cystatin C
biomarkers.description: Cystatin C is a filtration marker unaffected by muscle mass. At 0.82 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Beta-2-Microglobulin
biomarkers.description: Beta-2-microglobulin is cleared by the kidneys and rises with immune activation. At 1.30 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Urea
biomarkers.description: Urea is a protein waste product. At 2.77 it is within the laboratory range but below the 3.0 ideal, which usually reflects a modest protein intake; on a ketogenic diet aiming to build muscle, that is worth knowing.

biomarkers.name: Uric Acid
biomarkers.description: Uric acid rises with insulin resistance, fructose and alcohol. At 156 it is within the laboratory range but slightly below ideal, and it carries no concern; a low-carbohydrate diet without fructose keeps it low.

biomarkers.name: Neutrophil Gelatinase-Associated Lipocalin (NGAL)
biomarkers.description: NGAL rises with acute kidney injury. At 1259 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Kidney Assessment
biomarkers.description: Cystatin C 0.82, eGFR 111, urine albumin not detected, NGAL normal.

biomarkers.name: Kidney Injury Molecule-1 (KIM-1)
biomarkers.description: Kidney Injury Molecule-1 (KIM-1) is part of the Signature panel but was reported by Randox as not available on this sample. NGAL was returned and is normal, which covers the acute kidney injury question.

biomarkers.name: eGFR (Creatinine)
biomarkers.description: eGFR from creatinine alone, as reported by Randox. At 111 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: eGFR (Cystatin C)
biomarkers.description: eGFR estimated from cystatin C. Ideal. Cystatin C is unaffected by muscle mass, so this is the fairest kidney estimate.
biomarkers.low_causes: Chronic kidney disease, dehydration, kidney strain

biomarkers.name: eGFR (Creatinine + Cystatin C)
biomarkers.description: eGFR combining creatinine and cystatin C. Ideal. Both filtration estimates agree.
biomarkers.low_causes: Chronic kidney disease, dehydration, kidney strain

biomarkers.name: Urea:Creatinine Ratio
biomarkers.description: The urea to creatinine ratio. Within range; a low urea from modest protein intake, not a kidney finding.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low protein intake, liver disease, overhydration
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, high protein intake, upper GI bleeding

biomarkers.name: Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH)
biomarkers.description: TSH is the pituitary signal that drives the thyroid. At 1.16 it is ideal. The thyroid is not part of the fatigue or the large red cells.

biomarkers.name: Free Thyroxine (FT4)
biomarkers.description: FT4 is the storage thyroid hormone. At 17.2 it is ideal. Adequate storage hormone with a slightly low FT3 is the mild conversion slowdown that very low-carbohydrate diets produce, and it is harmless.

biomarkers.name: Free Tri-iodothyronine (FT3)
biomarkers.description: FT3 is the active thyroid hormone. At 4.40 it is within the laboratory range and just below the 4.5 ideal. Very low-carbohydrate diets lower FT3 slightly, and this level carries no concern with a perfect TSH.

biomarkers.name: Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG)
biomarkers.description: TBG carries thyroid hormone in the blood. At 14.2 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Thyroid Assessment
biomarkers.description: TSH 1.16, FT4 17.2, FT3 4.40, TBG 14.2, antibodies negative (anti-TPO 9.82, not zero). Not part of the fatigue.

biomarkers.name: FT3:FT4 Ratio
biomarkers.description: The FT3 to FT4 ratio reflects thyroid hormone conversion. Slightly below ideal, which a very low-carbohydrate diet does; no concern with a perfect TSH.
biomarkers.low_causes: Poor T4 to T3 conversion, low ferritin or selenium, chronic illness

biomarkers.name: TSH:FT4 Ratio
biomarkers.description: The TSH to FT4 ratio. Ideal. The pituitary is not having to push the thyroid at all.
biomarkers.high_causes: Pituitary working harder to maintain thyroid output

biomarkers.name: Creatine Kinase-MB (CK-MB)
biomarkers.description: CK-MB is the heart-muscle form of creatine kinase. Below 0.78 it is undetectable.

biomarkers.name: Creatine Kinase
biomarkers.description: Creatine kinase leaks from muscle after exertion. At 33 it is within range and at the low end, consistent with no resistance training.

biomarkers.name: Myoglobin
biomarkers.description: Myoglobin is released from damaged muscle. At 5.19 it is very low and ideal.

biomarkers.name: Troponin T
biomarkers.description: Troponin T is the most specific marker of heart muscle injury. Below 3 it is undetectable, which is exactly right.

biomarkers.name: Fatty Acid Binding Protein-3 (FABP-3)
biomarkers.description: FABP-3 rises early with heart muscle strain. At 1.55 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Haemolysis Screen
biomarkers.description: Haptoglobin 0.98 and LDH 293 within range. Her large red cells are a production problem (folate), not a destruction problem.

biomarkers.name: Cardiac Risk Assessment
biomarkers.description: Troponin T undetectable, CK-MB undetectable, myoglobin and FABP-3 ideal. No heart muscle stress.

biomarkers.name: H. pylori
biomarkers.description: H. pylori antibodies detect the stomach bacterium behind ulcers. Below 0.40 the result is negative.

biomarkers.name: Gastrin
biomarkers.description: Gastrin tells the stomach to make acid. At 9.87 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Digestive Assessment
biomarkers.description: H. pylori negative, coeliac negative (valid if eating gluten), gastrin 9.87, amylase 28, lipase 39.0. No digestive cause for the folate deficiency found; diet is the explanation.

biomarkers.name: Immunoglobulin E (IgE)
biomarkers.description: IgE is the allergy antibody. At 72.6 it is within the laboratory range but above the ideal, a mild allergic tendency.

biomarkers.name: Complement Component 3 (C3)
biomarkers.description: C3 is part of the complement system. At 1.05 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Complement Component 4 (C4)
biomarkers.description: The second complement marker. At 0.234 it is within range. Together with a normal C3 this makes lupus and immune-complex conditions unlikely.

biomarkers.name: Haptoglobin
biomarkers.description: Haptoglobin falls when red cells break down. At 0.98 it is within range, so there is no haemolysis behind the red cell changes.

biomarkers.name: Immunoglobulin A (IgA)
biomarkers.description: IgA guards the gut and airways. At 2.23 it is within range, which validates the coeliac test.

biomarkers.name: Immunoglobulin G (IgG)
biomarkers.description: The main long-term antibody class. At 11.16 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Immunoglobulin M (IgM)
biomarkers.description: The first antibody made in a new infection. At 1.39 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Epstein-Barr Nuclear Antigen (EBNA) IgG
biomarkers.description: EBNA IgG appears months after Epstein-Barr infection and stays for life. At 114 it is positive: past infection.

biomarkers.name: Epstein-Barr Viral Capsid Antigen (VCA) IgG
biomarkers.description: The long-term memory antibody to Epstein-Barr. At 69.2 it is positive, a past infection.

biomarkers.name: Epstein-Barr Viral Capsid Antigen (VCA) IgM
biomarkers.description: Appears in the first weeks of a new Epstein-Barr infection. At 0.41 it is negative, so nothing current.

biomarkers.name: Immune Assessment
biomarkers.description: Immunoglobulins, complement and antibodies all normal. IgE 72.6 within range but above ideal, a mild allergic tendency. Past Epstein-Barr infection only.

biomarkers.name: EBV Status
biomarkers.description: EBNA IgG 114 and VCA IgG 69.2 positive, VCA IgM 0.41 negative. Not active.

biomarkers.name: Anti-Tissue Transglutaminase Antibodies (Coeliac)
biomarkers.description: The coeliac antibody. At 0.5 it is negative with a normal IgA, so the result is valid. This matters here because coeliac disease is a cause of folate deficiency, and it has been excluded, provided she was eating some gluten; on a strict ketogenic diet she may not have been, which the GP should weigh.

biomarkers.name: Rheumatoid Factor (RF)
biomarkers.description: Rheumatoid factor. Below 6.72 it is negative. With anti-CCP also negative, rheumatoid arthritis is excluded.

biomarkers.name: Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide (Anti-CCP) Antibodies
biomarkers.description: The most specific antibody for rheumatoid arthritis. Below 8 it is negative.

biomarkers.name: Anti-Nuclear Antibodies (ANA)
biomarkers.description: The screening antibody for lupus and related conditions. Negative.

biomarkers.name: Intrinsic Factor Antibodies
biomarkers.description: Intrinsic factor antibodies cause pernicious anaemia, a form of B12 deficiency. Below 0.3 they are negative, so her below-ideal B12 is dietary, not autoimmune.

biomarkers.name: Gastric Parietal Cell Antibodies
biomarkers.description: The second marker for autoimmune gastritis. At 0.60 it is negative.

biomarkers.name: Anti-Thyroglobulin Antibody (Anti-Tg)
biomarkers.description: Thyroglobulin antibodies signal autoimmune thyroid disease. At 16.1 they are negative.

biomarkers.name: Anti-Thyroid Peroxidase Antibody (Anti-TPO)
biomarkers.description: TPO antibodies are the main marker of Hashimoto’s. At 9.82 they are below the 20 limit and negative, though not zero; with a perfect TSH this needs nothing now and is worth rechecking in a couple of years.

biomarkers.name: Autoimmune Assessment
biomarkers.description: ANA, RF, anti-CCP, coeliac, intrinsic factor, parietal cell and thyroid antibodies all negative; C3 and C4 normal.

biomarkers.name: Neuron Specific Enolase (NSE)
biomarkers.description: NSE is a screening marker associated with neuroendocrine tumours. At 19.98 it is within the laboratory range, in the upper half. It is a marker that varies considerably between samples, and within range it is a normal result.

biomarkers.name: Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP)
biomarkers.description: A screening marker for liver and germ cell tumours. At 2.5 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Carcinoembryonic Antigen (CEA)
biomarkers.description: A screening marker associated with bowel cancer. At 1.1 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Cancer Antigen 15-3 (CA 15-3)
biomarkers.description: A screening marker associated with breast cancer. At 14.5 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Cancer Antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9)
biomarkers.description: A screening marker associated with pancreatic cancer. At 8.5 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Cancer Antigen 125 (CA 125)
biomarkers.description: A screening marker associated with ovarian cancer, which also rises with endometriosis. At 12.6 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Human Chorionic Gonadotrophin (hCG)
biomarkers.description: The pregnancy hormone and a germ cell tumour marker. Below 0.2 it is negative.

biomarkers.name: Mesothelin
biomarkers.description: A screening marker associated with mesothelioma and ovarian cancer. Below 2.66 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Calcitonin
biomarkers.description: A screening marker for medullary thyroid cancer. At 2.95 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Cancer Screening Assessment
biomarkers.description: CA 125, CA 15-3, CA 19-9, CEA, AFP, hCG, calcitonin and mesothelin within range; NSE high in range for sample reasons. Screening support, not a diagnosis.

biomarkers.name: Total PSA
biomarkers.description: Prostate-specific antigen is not applicable to a female panel.

biomarkers.name: Prostate Cancer Risk Score
biomarkers.description: The prostate risk score is derived from PSA and is not applicable to a female panel. It is listed because it is part of the advertised Signature set.

biomarkers.name: Cardiovascular Risk Profile
biomarkers.description: The Cardiovascular Risk Score is 35 out of 100, in the acceptable band rather than the ideal band of 20 or below, and the only thing holding it there is Lp(a): ApoB 73, LDL 2.56, HDL 1.59, triglycerides 0.78 and hsCRP undetectable. Lp(a) at 40.2 is mildly above ideal and is the one inherited factor to keep in mind long term. The D-dimer is a clotting question, not a cholesterol one, and is handled separately.
biomarkers.result: Low to acceptable, one inherited note

biomarkers.name: Weight Target
biomarkers.description: Her BMI of 24.3 is already in the ideal range, so there is no weight target. The goal is body composition: more muscle at the same weight, through protein and resistance training.

biomarkers.name: BMI
biomarkers.description: Body mass index from her weight of 67 kg and height of 166 cm. At 24.3 it is within the ideal range.
biomarkers.high_causes: Excess body fat or high muscle mass

biomarkers.name: BMR
biomarkers.description: Basal metabolic rate, estimated with the Mifflin-St Jeor equation. A measurement, not a result.

biomarkers.name: TDEE
biomarkers.description: Total daily energy expenditure at her current activity level.

biomarkers.name: Body Fat % (estimated)
biomarkers.description: Body fat estimated from BMI, age and sex (Deurenberg). An estimate; the Signature appointment measurements are better.

biomarkers.name: Body Surface Area
biomarkers.description: Body surface area by the Du Bois formula. Used to scale some medication doses and kidney measures; a measurement, not a result.

biomarkers.name: Lean Body Mass (estimated)
biomarkers.description: Estimated lean mass. Building this is her goal, and it needs protein and resistance training more than any change to the diet’s carbohydrate.

biomarkers.name: Fat Mass (estimated)
biomarkers.description: Estimated fat mass. Within a healthy range for her height. Her goal is to add muscle at this weight rather than lose fat.

biomarkers.name: Protein Target
biomarkers.description: About 105 grams of protein a day, roughly 1.6 grams per kilogram, which is the level that supports building muscle at 49; her urea suggests she is currently below it.

biomarkers.name: Calorie Target
biomarkers.description: Around 1,700 calories a day at maintenance for her current weight and activity. With a BMI of 24.3 the goal is body composition, not weight loss.

biomarkers.name: Bilirubin (Urine)
biomarkers.description: Bilirubin in urine would suggest a liver or bile problem. Negative.

biomarkers.name: Glucose (Urine)
biomarkers.description: Glucose in urine appears once blood sugar is high. Negative, which with the HbA1c of 33 confirms healthy sugar control.

biomarkers.name: Ketones (Urine)
biomarkers.description: Ketones in urine show the body burning fat for fuel. At 15 mg/dl they are present, which is the expected and intended state on a ketogenic diet. It is not a concern with a normal HbA1c and bicarbonate.

biomarkers.name: Nitrite (Urine)
biomarkers.description: Nitrite suggests a urinary infection. Negative. With white cells also negative there is no urinary infection.

biomarkers.name: pH (Urine)
biomarkers.description: Urine pH reflects acidity. At 6.0 it is within range. A mildly acidic urine is consistent with ketones being excreted on a ketogenic diet.

biomarkers.name: Protein (Urine)
biomarkers.description: Protein in urine suggests kidney strain. Negative. Together with an undetectable urine albumin, the kidney filters are intact.

biomarkers.name: Red Blood Cells (Urine)
biomarkers.description: Red cells in urine suggest bleeding in the urinary tract. Negative.

biomarkers.name: Urobilinogen (Urine)
biomarkers.description: A normal breakdown product. At 0.2 it is normal. Normal levels confirm bile pigments are being processed and excreted as expected.

biomarkers.name: White Blood Cells (Urine)
biomarkers.description: White cells in urine suggest infection. Negative. With nitrite also negative there is no infection to explain the neutrophil count.

biomarkers.name: Calculated Free Testosterone
biomarkers.description: Free testosterone calculated from total testosterone, SHBG and albumin. Within range at the low end, because SHBG is high; more relevant to her muscle-building goal than the total.

biomarkers.name: Bioavailable Testosterone
biomarkers.description: Testosterone available to tissues. At the low end for the same reason.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low total testosterone, high SHBG, obesity, poor sleep, chronic stress

biomarkers.name: Free Oestradiol Index
biomarkers.description: The free oestradiol index. Reported for context; oestradiol is a healthy mid-cycle level.

biomarkers.name: LH:FSH Ratio
biomarkers.description: The LH to FSH ratio. At 0.54 it is within range, an early-cycle pattern.
biomarkers.high_causes: Pattern seen in polycystic ovary syndrome

biomarkers.name: Mentzer Index
biomarkers.description: The Mentzer index separates iron deficiency from thalassaemia trait using MCV and red cell count. High, which with normal iron stores simply reflects the macrocytosis of folate deficiency.

biomarkers.name: Monocyte-to-Lymphocyte Ratio
biomarkers.description: The monocyte to lymphocyte ratio. Within the ideal range. A normal monocyte to lymphocyte balance argues against chronic immune activation.

biomarkers.name: Lymphocyte-to-Monocyte Ratio
biomarkers.description: The lymphocyte to monocyte ratio. Within the ideal range. The inverse view of the same balance, also within ideal.

biomarkers.name: Neutrophil-to-Monocyte Ratio
biomarkers.description: The neutrophil to monocyte ratio. Within range. Neutrophils are high in range only because of short sleep and an afternoon draw.
